score_1_desc:
<20% of inbound trucks arrive against a pre-booked slot.
>50% of daily volume clusters into a single 2-hour window, causing dock queuing beyond 2 hours.
No designated driver holding area - drivers and helpers congregate at the security gate causing congestion.
Dock-in time is not captured, so it cannot feed downstream Goods Receipt Note (GRN) turnaround-time (TAT) SLAs.
Slot booking, where it exists, is a manual register entry with no Quick Response (QR)/Booking-ID confirmation shared with the vendor ahead of arrival.
score_2_desc:
20-50% slot adherence.
Peak-hour concentration still exceeds 40% of daily volume.
Average vehicle wait time 60-120 minutes.
An informal holding area exists but is not enforced, so congregation at the gate persists.
Dock-in time is logged manually but not used to track GRN TAT.
A digital slot booking exists for under 30% of vendors, without a QR/Booking-ID confirmation shared back to the vendor.
score_3_desc:
50-75% slot adherence via a basic appointment scheduler.
Peak-hour concentration reduced to 25-40%.
Average wait time 30-60 minutes.
A designated driver holding area away from the security gate is marked and used for the majority of vehicles.
Dock-in time is captured and reviewed, but not yet formalized as an Service Level Agreement (SLA) input for GRN TAT.
A digital slot booking with a QR/Booking-ID confirmation (D-2 indent leading to a D-1 slot) is shared with 30-60% of vendors ahead of arrival.
score_4_desc:
75-90% slot adherence with system-enforced windows.
Peak-hour concentration under 25%.
Average wait time under 30 minutes.
Adherence tracked daily.
The driver holding area is enforced with signage/marshalling, keeping the security gate clear.
Dock-in time is captured digitally and used as the starting SLA clock for downstream GRN TAT.
Digital slot booking with a QR/Booking-ID confirmation (D-2 indent to D-1 slot) is shared with 60-90% of vendors, scanned at the gate to authenticate arrival.
score_5_desc:
>90% slot adherence with automated vendor notification.
Load spread within +/-10% across all shift hours.
Average wait time under 15 minutes.
zero congregation at the security gate.
Dock-in time is system-captured and forms the auditable SLA start-point for GRN TAT, with automated breach alerts.
Digital slot booking with a QR/Booking-ID confirmation (D-2 indent to D-1 slot) is shared with over 90% of vendors and scanned at the gate as the primary authentication step, with zero manual slot entries.
indicative_scoring_questions:
• Is there a defined slot-booking mechanism for inbound vehicles? What % arrive within their booked slot?
• What % of daily inbound volume clusters into a single peak window, and what is the average vehicle wait time?
• Is a designated driver holding area (away from the security gate) marked and enforced?
• Is dock-in time captured, and does it feed the Goods Receipt Note (GRN) turnaround-time (TAT) Service Level Agreement (SLA)?
• Is slot booking digital, with a Quick Response (QR)/Booking-ID sent to vendors ahead of arrival and scanned at the gate?

score_1_desc:
<50% of gate entries verified against indent/invoice before unloading starts (across the 70:30 vendor:courier vehicle mix, with no differentiated checklist for vendor vs courier vehicles).
Documentation/invoice mismatch rate above 30%.
Average gate-in time over 20 min/vehicle.
There is no driver-ID or vehicle-number authentication against the booked slot, and temperature checks (where done at all) are not scoped to any specific Stock-Keeping Unit (SKU) or deviation threshold.
score_2_desc:
50-70% verified pre-unload, using a single generic checklist applied to both vendor (70% of vehicle mix) and courier (30% of vehicle mix) vehicles.
Mismatch rate 20-30%.
Gate-in time 15-20 min/vehicle.
Driver-ID and vehicle-number are checked against the slot for under 30% of vehicles.
A temperature check is performed inconsistently and without a defined deviation threshold, even for 4°C-sensitive SKUs (e.g., mushrooms).
score_3_desc:
70-85% verified against a defined checklist (vendor, invoice, indented qty, reefer temperature), with separate verification steps for vendor trucks (70% of vehicle mix) and courier vans (30% of vehicle mix).
Mismatch rate 10-20%.
Gate-in time 10-15 min.
Driver-ID and vehicle-number are authenticated against the vendor code, Purchase Order (PO), and slot for 30-60% of vehicles.
Temperature is checked specifically for 4°C-sensitive SKUs (e.g., mushrooms,apples etc) but the reject threshold (e.g., >3°C deviation) is not consistently applied.
score_4_desc:
85-95% verified via system-assisted matching (barcode/Optical Character Recognition (OCR)) across both vendor (70% of vehicle mix) and courier (30% of vehicle mix) vehicle streams.
Mismatch rate 5-10%.
Gate-in time 5-10 min.
100% of reefer vehicles temperature-logged.
Driver-ID and vehicle-number authentication against vendor code, PO, and slot covers 60-90% of vehicles.
A defined temperature-reject rule (>3°C deviation for 4°C-sensitive SKUs such as mushrooms only, not the full FnV range) is applied consistently.
score_5_desc:
>95% verified end-to-end digitally with zero manual entry, with vendor (70% of vehicle mix) and courier (30% of vehicle mix) streams tracked and matched separately.
Mismatch rate under 5%.
Gate-in time under 5 min.
Full audit trail with automated exception flags.
Driver-ID and vehicle-number authentication against vendor code, PO, and slot covers over 90% of vehicles with zero exceptions.
The >3°C-deviation temperature-reject rule, scoped only to 4°C-sensitive SKUs (e.g., mushrooms), is enforced with zero missed checks and logged as part of the gate audit trail.
indicative_scoring_questions:
• What % of gate entries are verified against indent/invoice before unloading starts?
• Is there a separate verification checklist for vendor vehicles vs courier vehicles (given the typical 70:30 mix)?
• What is the documentation/invoice mismatch rate, and average gate-in time per vehicle?
• Is driver-ID and vehicle-number authenticated against the vendor code, Purchase Order (PO), and booked slot?
• Is temperature checked for temperature-sensitive Stock-Keeping Units (SKUs) (e.g., mushrooms), with a defined deviation reject threshold (e.g., >3°C)?

score_1_desc:
Gate operates as a security checkpoint, 
trucks are waved onto the dock/yard regardless of whether a dock bay or staging space is available, with no reject / temp-reject / hold / bypass decision rule (checks vary guard-to-guard).
Gate-out has no exit slip or outbound-seal verification. Vehicles routinely block the dock and back up into S&G congestion.
score_2_desc:
A capacity check is attempted informally for under 30% of gate-ins (e.g., a phone call to the dock supervisor or physical check) with no defined time window, so vehicles sent to hold still cause dock-blocking regularly.
Reject/hold decisions depend on individual guard judgment.
Gate-out has no formal exit slip or seal check.
score_3_desc:
A defined capacity check (dock bay + staging pallet positions available within a stated window, e.g., 15 minutes) gates 30-60% of gate-ins, routing 'no' decisions to the holding area.
A basic reject-vs-hold rule exists, but temp-reject (scoped to 4°C SKUs) and bypass-routing (pre-packed vendors) are not yet part of the same decision rule.
Gate-out issues an exit slip for the majority of dispatches but outbound emptyness of return to vendor(RTV) is not checked
score_4_desc:
Capacity-gated release (dock bay + staging space confirmed within 15 minutes) governs 60-90% of gate-ins.
The full reject / temp-reject / hold / bypass decision  is defined and applied consistently, with 'hold' vehicles routed to the designated holding area.
Gate-out issues an exit slip and verifies the outbound vehicle are empty or have only the RTV material for the majority of dispatches.
Physical enablers (multi-lane entry, boom barrier, Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV)/tablet at the gate) are in place.
score_5_desc:
Over 90% of gate-ins are capacity-gated in real time (dock bay + staging space confirmed within 15 minutes, tied live to the dock-management and staging systems), with zero blind releases and zero dock-blocking incidents.
The full reject / temp-reject / hold / bypass decision is applied with a complete audit trail.
Gate-out is fully controlled (exit slip plus outbound  verification on 100% of dispatches).
Physical enablers (multi-lane entry with boom barrier, CCTV/tablet where applicable) are fully deployed.
indicative_scoring_questions:
• Is a capacity check (dock bay + staging space availability within a defined time window) performed before releasing a vehicle onto the dock?
• Is there a defined reject/temp-reject/hold/bypass decision rule, applied consistently rather than left to individual guard judgment?
• What % of gate-ins are capacity-gated, and are dock-blocking incidents tracked?
• Is an exit slip issued at gate-out, and is the outbound vehicle checked for empty or Return to Vendor (RTV)-only load?
• Are physical enablers (multi-lane entry, boom barrier, Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV)/tablet) in place at the gate?

score_1_desc:
0% biometric/facial recognition coverage at shift changeovers.
Manual register only, with no zone-wise capturing of manpower entries (e.g., S&G, packing, put-away, dispatch) against planned manpower
Unauthorized-entry incidents exceed 60 per month.
score_2_desc:
Under 30% biometric coverage.
Manual plus partial physical checks.
Zone-wise entry counts recorded ad hoc for under 30% of zones, not benchmarked against a  manpower plan.
Unauthorized-entry incidents 30-60 per month.
score_3_desc:
30-60% facial recognition coverage at main shift changeovers.
Zone-wise manpower entry tracked for 30-60% of zones (e.g., S&G, packing, put-away) against a defined headcount  ( e.g., ~10 for S&G, ~25 for packing), reviewed daily.
Unauthorized-entry incidents 10-30 per month.
score_4_desc:
60-90% coverage across all shifts and gates.
Zone-wise entry captured and reconciled daily for 60-90% of zones against the warehouse-sizing-based manpower plan, integrated with the attendance system.
Unauthorized-entry incidents under 10 per month, zero incidents in the last quarter.
score_5_desc:
100% facial recognition and physical-check coverage across all shifts and gates.
Zone-wise manpower entry captured in real time for 100% of zones, with automated variance alerts against the warehouse-sizing-based headcount plan.
Zero unauthorized-entry incidents in the last 12 months.
Real-time anomaly alerts.
indicative_scoring_questions:
• What % of shift changeovers are covered by biometric/facial-recognition entry checks?
• Is manpower entry tracked zone-wise (e.g., Sorting & Grading (S&G), packing, put-away, dispatch) against a defined headcount plan?
• How many unauthorized-entry incidents occur per month?
• Is zone-wise entry reconciled daily or in real time, with variance alerts against the manpower plan?

score_1_desc:
No formal dock allocation system.
Dock utilization under 50%.
Docks unnumbered or inconsistently numbered.
score_2_desc:
Manual dock allocation sheet.
Utilization 50-65%.
Docks numbered in the past but not visible or signages are missing
score_3_desc:
Defined dock allocation by vehicle size with numbered docks.
Utilization 65-80%.
First-In-First-Out (FIFO) followed for over 70% of vehicles.
score_4_desc:
System-based dock scheduling with size-matched allocation.
Utilization 80-90%.
FIFO adherence above 90%.
Green-channel vehicles wait time within 15 minutes.
score_5_desc:
Fully automated dock-vehicle matching with real-time queuing.
Utilization above 90%.
FIFO adherence 100%.
Green-channel wait time under 10 minutes.
indicative_scoring_questions:
• Is there a formal dock allocation system, and are docks clearly numbered and signed?
• What is current dock utilization % (dock-hours occupied / available dock-hours)?
• Is dock allocation matched to vehicle size?
• What % of vehicles are handled First-In-First-Out (FIFO)?
• Is there a green-channel lane for priority vehicles, and what is its wait time?

score_1_desc:
Under 25% of docks fitted with buffers.
More than 1 dock-damage incident per week.
No penalty framework for drivers causing repeat dock damage.
Physical damage to dock structures not tracked or inspected separately from buffer coverage.
score_2_desc:
25-50% buffer coverage.
1 dock-damage incident per week on average.
Repeat-offender drivers flagged informally but no defined penalty applied.
Physical dock-structure damage noted only when reported by staff, with no periodic inspection.
score_3_desc:
50-75% buffer coverage.
1 dock-damage incident every 2 weeks.
A defined penalty (e.g., warning/fine) applied to drivers on a repeat incident.
Physical dock-structure damage inspected monthly and logged separately from buffer-related damage.
score_4_desc:
75-95% buffer coverage.
Fewer than 1 dock-damage incident every 4 weeks.
A graded penalty scale (warning, fine, vendor/transporter review) enforced for repeat-offender drivers.
Periodic buffer-condition audits in place.
Physical dock-structure damage inspected weekly with defects tracked to closure.
score_5_desc:
100% dock buffer coverage.
Zero damage incidents in the last 12 months.
Graded penalty scale for repeat-offender drivers strictly enforced with under 2% repeat-offense rate.
Preventive maintenance schedule tracked.
Zero unresolved physical dock-structure damage, verified via weekly inspection.
indicative_scoring_questions:
• What % of docks are fitted with protective buffers?
• How many dock-damage incidents occur per week?
• Is there a defined, graded penalty framework (warning, fine, vendor/transporter review) for drivers causing repeat dock damage, and is it enforced?
• Is physical dock-structure damage (separate from buffer wear) inspected on a periodic schedule, with defects tracked to closure?

score_1_desc:
No defined/target unloading Service Level Agreement (SLA).
No dock-wise dedicated workforce assigned.
No defined palletisation zone (material is palletized wherever space is available, creating space constraints at the inbound gate).
No crate-stacking pattern defined (poor vertical space utilization).
Waste (e.g., vegetable trimmings) accumulates at the entry gate.
No separate lane/green-channel for reliable vendors or for dry-category inbound.
No bypass-routing flag exists for vendor pre-packed material, so pre-packed loads are routed through S&G by default regardless of need.
score_2_desc:
An unloading SLA is defined but tracked for under 30% of docks (benchmark: ~500 units/person/hour for pre-packed material or 5 pallets/person/hour or 150 crates/person/hour).
Dock-wise workforce assignment is informal.
A palletisation zone is nominally marked but frequently encroached upon.
Crate stacking has no defined Standard Operating Procedure (SOP).
Waste disposal remains near the inbound gate.
A bypass flag for vendor pre-packed material is used informally for under 30% of eligible loads.
score_3_desc:
Unloading SLA(benchmark: ~500 units/person/hour for pre-packed material or 5 pallets/person/hour or 150 crates/person/hour) is tracked for 30-60% of docks with a dock-wise supervisor-led team.
A visibly marked palletisation zone and sorting/grading area are maintained on most days.
A crate-stacking SOP (max stack height, brick/inline pattern) is defined but followed inconsistently.
A green channel exists for some reliable vendors.
Waste disposal has been relocated away from the inbound gate.
A bypass-routing flag for vendor pre-packed material, skipping S&G and routing straight to packing/staging, is applied for 30-60% of eligible loads.
score_4_desc:
Unloading SLA is tracked for 60-90% of docks against benchmark(benchmark: ~500 units/person/hour for pre-packed material or 5 pallets/person/hour or 150 crates/person/hour), with a dock-wise supervisor-led team on every shift.
Palletisation zone, unloading area, and S&G area are marked and adhered to.
Crate-stacking SOP is followed on 70-95% of pallets.
A green channel is consistently used for reliable vendors.
First-In-First-Out (FIFO) lanes for S&G are marked on the floor.
Dry-category inbound, if any , has a defined separate lane.
The bypass-routing flag for vendor pre-packed material is applied for 60-90% of eligible loads, tracked as part of the load-declaration step at gate/weighment.
score_5_desc:
Unloading SLA is tracked for over 90% of docks and consistently meets/exceeds the benchmark((benchmark: ~500 units/person/hour for pre-packed material or 5 pallets/person/hour or 150 crates/person/hour), with a dock-wise supervisor-led team at all times.
Palletisation zone, unloading area, and S&G area are marked, audited, and adhered to with zero space-constraint incidents.
Crate-stacking SOP compliance exceeds 95%.
Green-channel and dry-category lanes operate with zero cross-flow incidents.
Waste is cleared from a defined point on a fixed schedule.
The bypass-routing flag for vendor pre-packed material is applied for over 90% of eligible loads with zero mis-routes, fully integrated into the load-declaration and Goods Receipt Note (GRN)-generation step.
indicative_scoring_questions:
• Is an unloading productivity Service Level Agreement (SLA) defined and tracked by dock (benchmark ~500 units/person/hour, 5 pallets/person/hour, or 150 crates/person/hour)?
• Is there a dedicated, dock-wise supervisor-led workforce for unloading?
• Are the palletisation, unloading, and Sorting & Grading (S&G) zones clearly marked and free of space-constraint/encroachment incidents?
• Is a crate-stacking Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) (max height, pattern) defined and followed?
• Is waste (e.g., vegetable trimmings) cleared from the inbound gate area on a fixed schedule?
• Is a bypass-routing flag used to route vendor pre-packed material straight to packing/staging (skipping S&G), and is it tracked at gate/weighment?

score_1_desc:
Unloading Turnaround Time (TAT) (dock-in to unloading-complete) exceeds 90 minutes per vehicle on average.
Unloading is frequently not initiated at all after dock-in - vehicles sit docked with no unloading action for extended periods.
No distinction is made between slow unloading and unloading never started.
score_2_desc:
Unloading TAT averages 60-90 minutes per vehicle.
Unloading-not-initiated cases still occur but are not tracked separately from slow-unloading cases.
score_3_desc:
Unloading TAT averages 40-60 minutes per vehicle, tracked per vehicle for the majority of dock-ins.
Unloading-not-initiated incidents are logged separately from TAT and reviewed occasionally.
score_4_desc:
Unloading TAT averages 25-40 minutes per vehicle, tracked per vehicle and reviewed daily against the unloading Service Level Agreement (SLA).
Unloading is initiated within a defined time of dock-in for the majority of vehicles, with unloading-not-initiated incidents root-caused weekly.
score_5_desc:
Unloading TAT is held under 25 minutes per vehicle for over 90% of dock-ins, tracked in real time and feeding the Dock-to-Stock Time Key Performance Indicator (KPI).
Unloading is initiated promptly per SLA for every dock-in, with zero unloading-not-initiated incidents.
indicative_scoring_questions:
• What is the average Unloading Turnaround Time (TAT) (dock-in to unloading-complete), per vehicle?
• Are unloading-not-initiated incidents (vehicle docked but unloading never starts) tracked separately from slow-unloading cases?
• Is unloading TAT reviewed against a defined Service Level Agreement (SLA), and how often (occasional/weekly/daily/real-time)?
• Does unloading TAT feed the Dock-to-Stock Time Key Performance Indicator (KPI)?

score_1_desc:
Weighment data is logged manually for Goods Receipt Note (GRN)/Purchase Order (PO) creation - error-prone and slow.
Weighment occurs both upstream and downstream of S&G, increasing vendor wait time and delaying PO closure.
The weighment area sits hard against the staging area with no clear aisle, creating a choke point.
Scale calibration is untracked.
score_2_desc:
Manual logging accounts for over 70% of weighment transactions.
Weighment is still performed both pre and post-S&G 
The clear aisle between weighment and staging is under 1.8m or undefined.
Scale calibration is done ad hoc with no fixed schedule.
score_3_desc:
Digital weighment is integrated with the Warehouse Management System (WMS)/GRN system for 30-60% of transactions.
Weighment has been shifted to the only after S&G,thus reducing double weighment.
A minimum 1.8m clear aisle between weighment and staging is maintained on most days.
Scales are calibrated on a defined but not strictly daily schedule.
score_4_desc:
Digital weighment integrated with WMS/GRN covers 60-90% of transactions.
Weighment is performed at the after S&G stage for the majority of vendors, except the leafies.
The 1.8m clear-aisle buffer between weighment and staging is consistently maintained.
Calibrated scales with tare memory per packaging type are recalibrated on a defined schedule (daily recommended).
Digital weight logs are retained as an audit trail.
score_5_desc:
Over 90% of weighment transactions are digitally integrated with WMS/GRN with zero manual entry.
Weighment is performed at the unloading stage for all applicable vendors, enabling same-day PO closure.
The 1.8m clear-aisle buffer is maintained with zero choke-point incidents.
Scales are recalibrated daily with tare memory per packaging type.
The digital weight log is used as a routine audit trail for supplier invoice reconciliation and shrinkage analysis.
indicative_scoring_questions:
• What % of weighment transactions are digitally integrated with the Warehouse Management System (WMS)/Goods Receipt Note (GRN), vs manually logged?
• Is weighment performed before or after Sorting & Grading (S&G), and has double weighment been eliminated?
• Is a minimum clear aisle (~1.8m) maintained between the weighment area and staging area?
• Are scales calibrated on a defined schedule (ideally daily), with tare memory set per packaging type?
• Is the digital weight log retained and used as an audit trail (e.g., invoice reconciliation, shrinkage analysis)?

score_1_desc:
No defined size or quality standards (blemish-free, rot-free, infestation-free) for sorting/grading.
Criteria applied on 0% of SKUs.
No S&G throughput Service Level Agreement (SLA) is defined (benchmark: ~250-300 units/person/hour for general S&G, 400-500 units/person/shift for leafy cutting).
Piece-category SKUs (e.g., coconut, watermelon) are staffed randomly, causing significant throughput slowdown.
score_2_desc:
Standards defined for under 30% of SKUs.
A throughput SLA is defined but tracked for under 30% of stations, with wide variance against the ~250 units/person/hour / 400-500 units/person/shift benchmarks.
Piece-category SKUs are not assigned to experienced manpower.
score_3_desc:
Standards defined for 30-60% of SKUs, covering blemish, rot, infestation, and size checks.
Throughput SLA (~250 units/person/hour, 400-500/shift for leafy) is tracked for 30-60% of stations.
Experienced manpower is assigned to piece-category SKUs (coconut, watermelon) only inconsistently.
score_4_desc:
Standards defined for 60-90% of SKUs, with grading accuracy audited monthly at over 90% accuracy.
Throughput SLA is tracked for 60-90% of stations, mostly within benchmark.
Experienced manpower is consistently assigned their specialisation article ,to maximise the throughput
score_5_desc:
Standards defined for 100% of SKUs.
Grading accuracy above 95%, audited weekly with a corrective feedback loop.
Throughput SLA is tracked for 100% of stations and consistently meets or exceeds benchmark (~250 units/person/hour, 400-500/shift leafy).
Experienced manpower is consistently assigned their specialisation article ,to maximise the throughput
indicative_scoring_questions:
• Are defined size/quality standards (blemish-free, rot-free, infestation-free) documented, and for what % of Stock-Keeping Units (SKUs) are they applied?
• Is a Sorting & Grading (S&G) throughput Service Level Agreement (SLA) defined and tracked against benchmark (~250-300 units/person/hour, or 400-500 packets/person/shift for leafy items)?
• Is grading accuracy audited, at what frequency, and what accuracy % is achieved?
• Are experienced/specialized staff consistently assigned to piece-category SKUs (e.g., coconut, watermelon)?

score_1_desc:
No standard manpower norm for processing tables.
Occupancy varies randomly (under 2 or over 6 people per 8ft x 4ft table).
No defined ratio of S&G tables to packaging tables hampering banalcing of processes - S&G tables are frequently fewer than packing tables, bottlenecking downstream packaging input.
No cleaning step is enforced between vendors' S&G batches, causing clutter/wastage accumulation and cross-contamination risk.
score_2_desc:
Norm defined (4 people per 8ft x 4ft table) but followed on under 40% of tables.
An S&G-to-packing table ratio is loosely followed for under 40% of shifts, with S&G output frequently under-matched to packing input hampering balancing of processes
Inter-vendor S&G, cleaning is ad hoc.
score_3_desc:
4-person-per-table norm followed on 40-70% of tables.
S&G-to-packing table ratio is matched to keep S&G output aligned with packing input on 40-70% of shifts.
Cleaning between vendors' S&G batches is performed inconsistently.
score_4_desc:
Norm followed on 70-95% of tables, monitored via regular floor walks.
S&G-to-packing table ratio and output-input matching is maintained on 70-95% of shifts, monitored via floor walks.
Cleaning after each vendor's S&G batch is standard practice.
score_5_desc:
Norm followed on over 95% of tables at all times, with real-time floor supervision preventing congestion or under-utilization.
S&G-to-packing table ratio and output-input matching is maintained on over 95% of shifts with real-time supervision.
Cleaning after every vendor's S&G batch is enforced with zero cross-contamination incidents.
indicative_scoring_questions:
• Is there a defined manpower norm per processing table (e.g., 4 people per 8ft x 4ft table), and what % of tables follow it?
• Is the ratio of Sorting & Grading (S&G) tables to packing tables managed to keep S&G output matched to packing input?
• Is a cleaning step enforced between different vendors' S&G batches?
• Is table occupancy monitored via regular floor walks or real-time supervision?

score_1_desc:
Packaging material (nets/boxes/Low-Density Polyethylene (LDPE)) not defined by Stock-Keeping Unit (SKU).
No packing method/Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) defined.
Formed boxes are stacked directly on the worktop, causing clutter.
Vendor-packed SKUs are routinely re-packed on arrival regardless of pack quality.
Chilled-category SKUs (e.g., apples, pears) are packed under ambient conditions with no dedicated chilled station.
score_2_desc:
Packaging material defined for under 50% of SKUs.
A packing method/SOP exists informally, not documented.
A formed-box staging shelf is used on under 30% of lines.
Vendor-pack alignment to Fulfillment Center (FC) standards covers under 30% of applicable vendors.
Chilled SKUs are packed ambient on over 70% of shifts.
score_3_desc:
Packaging material defined per SKU.
A documented packing method/SOP is followed on 30-60% of lines.
A formed-box staging shelf decongests the worktop on 30-60% of lines.
30-60% of applicable vendors pack to FC standard, removing the re-pack step.
A dedicated chilled packing station is used for 30-60% of chilled-SKU shifts.
score_4_desc:
Packaging material and packing method/SOP are defined and followed on 60-90% of lines.
Formed-box staging shelf standard is followed on 60-90% of lines.
60-90% of applicable vendors pack to standard.
A dedicated chilled packing station is used for 60-90% of chilled-SKU shifts.
score_5_desc:
Packaging material and packing method/SOP are defined and followed on all lines.
Formed-box staging shelf standard is followed on all lines.
Over 90% of applicable vendors pack to standard with zero re-pack sub-process.
100% of chilled SKUs are packed at a dedicated chilled station, audited monthly.
indicative_scoring_questions:
• Is packaging material (nets/boxes/Low-Density Polyethylene (LDPE)) defined per Stock-Keeping Unit (SKU), and is a packing method/Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) documented?
• Is a formed-box staging shelf used to keep the worktop decongested?
• What % of applicable vendors pack to Fulfillment Center (FC) standard, avoiding a re-pack step on arrival?
• Is there a dedicated chilled packing station for chilled-category SKUs (e.g., apples, pears), and is it audited?

score_1_desc:
Packing productivity under 60 units/person/hour.
No shift-level Service Level Agreement (SLA) tracked against category benchmarks (net roll ~90/hr, punnet ~100/hr, Low-Density Polyethylene (LDPE) bags ~100/hr).
Leafy gang output is not tracked against the 400-500 packets/person/day benchmark.
score_2_desc:
Productivity 60-80 units/person/hour.
Shift-level SLA is tracked for under 30% of lines against category benchmarks.
Leafy gang output is not benchmarked against the 400-500 packets/person/day target.
score_3_desc:
Productivity at the 80-100 units/person/hour benchmark band.
Shift-level SLA is tracked for 30-60% of lines and trending toward category benchmarks.
Leafy gang output is tracked against the 400-500 packets/person/day target for some shifts.
score_4_desc:
Productivity 100-120 units/person/hour, matching category benchmarks (net roll ~90/hr, punnet ~100/hr, LDPE bags ~100/hr).
Shift-level SLA is tracked for 60-90% of lines and mostly at benchmark.
Leafy gang output is tracked daily against the 400-500 packets/person/day target, with a 4-cutter + 6-packer gang trending toward 4,000+ packets/day.
score_5_desc:
Productivity above 120 units/person/hour, or consistently at the top of the category benchmark.
Shift-level SLA is tracked for over 90% of lines and consistently at or above benchmark.
A 4-cutter + 6-packer leafy gang achieves 4,000+ packets/day, tracked and improved monthly.
Productivity at this level confirms packing material and method (Packing Norms) are also mature.
indicative_scoring_questions:

GRN approval is procedurally linked to quality-team clearance, but clearance is manual/paper-based, not a system hold.
